blocks.x: August Lanois a while and I'll be back later. We'll try to put this right here on the, this little stool and hope that'll pick up everything. You mind telling just when you were born,
your birth date, and just where it was? Born in Yaws in 1902. What part of the city? The Garden District. Born on Philippine, Bernoulli.
What was the exact date? 1902. Of your birthday, the month and date? Oh, August the 13th. August the 13th. August the 13th, 1902.
Like me, I was born on the 13th too, June the 13th.
Can you tell us a little bit about your family, if your father played any instruments? My father was a guitar player. And he worked with any bands?
Well, there's one man that he worked with, was very famous, but he was a violinist. Oh, I can't think of that man's name now. He was very famous.
Robichaud, any chance? No, no, no. Or P. Rohn?
I can't think of that man's name right now. No, he was way back, way before those fellas.
Jimmy Palau? No. Or Jimmy Palau? No.
I mean, no. Got his name on the end of my tongue.
There was one old man, Valto.
That's it. Not Valto.
Or Palau? Jimmy Palau? No. It may come to you later, so don't worry about it. Your father played guitar, any other instruments then?
No, that's all. Just the guitar.
Anybody else in the family? Did your mother play anything? No, no, I didn't play. I wonder if she might have played piano or did she sing or anything?
Didn't play. Not the rest of the family.
Have any brothers or?

I have brothers, but none of them didn't take up no music. And I didn't take up music until around 1919. At that time I was around 17, 17 years old. And I started on the trombone. The trombone. And I was taking lessons from Professor J.B. Humphrey. Oh yes. Jim Humphrey. Jim Humphrey.
I was going to ask you about your first instrument. Did you happen to have a trombone around? How did you happen to settle on that instrument? Did your...

Well, I tell you, I had a cousin. He was a client at Flair. And he's the one who urged me to start music. Well, he had an old violin. He gave it to me. So I went to old man Hoffrey. And he told me, he said, you're wasting your time fooling around with an instrument like this. He said, because this instrument is not dying out. It's done dying out. So he advised me to take up the trombone. So that's why you settled on that. That's why I settled on the trombone.
What was your cousin's name, the Clarinet player?
Uh, Albert Gabriel. Oh yeah.
I think I would.

You called him Dude. Dude. Yeah, he was formerly from Algiers. Well, he wasn't exactly my cousin. He was my wife's cousin. You see. And, but when I met up with my wife, and the family, her family, she played piano. And her daddy played trumpet. Her brother was a drummer at that time. Well, now he's playing saxophone. He don't live there. He's a little drummer. And the rest of them, well, they were too small. But I have a brother in law. He plays piano. He used to play band jazz. But you know, we played with Louis DeMaine.
Oh yeah.
And just by getting into that family, that's how I started on that music.
What was your wife's father's name? Gabriel.
He was born in Gabriel.
Well, he was, there were all that big...

The trumpet, that's the one on that picture there. The trumpet player. Yeah. He had the national jazz office right at that time. Around 1918, up until about 1920, well, around 1930, I think he was still playing.
Yeah, he was.
We used to play with him, and then we played with others. Then there was two brothers and myself who formed a trio. We played all around. Trials? Trials was, wasn't famous. We had a trio.
What did you, what are your instruments?
Banjo, bass, and clarinet. Oh, that's... You played the bass at that time? Yeah, we played at Victors out here. Oh yeah. On, I think it was the charter and tools. Yeah, still there.
Well, we played about two years. Well, I was going to ask some more about your lessons with Jim Humphrey. Well. How often did you go? Oh, I used to go twice a week.
Twice a week.
Where did they teach? At his home, or where did he live up from?
At his home. He lived on, in the 4500 block on Liberty Street.
Way uptown. Mm-hmm. How much did you charge for a lesson, do you remember? 50 cents. 50? Those are private lessons or... Private. Not a class? No, private lessons.
He had an orchestra. And the orchestra had... Used to go around to different ones' houses and they'd practice each week.
Mm-hmm.
Every day they had a certain night. They'd go and the club used to furnish the refreshments.
Yeah.
Well, they didn't have nothing but cake and ice cream and salt drinks, something like that.
Yeah. Like a party would make out.

Yeah. And each week, the different students would meet. Those would, well, you know, were advanced enough to play in the officers. Yeah. And then they would probably play at maybe some church benefit or something like that. All right. They had a house party. And some of the club members' houses and different things all the time.
I wondered if you remembered anything else about your lessons, any of what method you used on your combo?
I used the coral fishing.

Coral fishing. Coral fishing. I think. Anything in particular about his teaching, how he made you count or whether you had to sing the numbers first or anything? What did he have you to do? He had to sing the numbers.
And count. They taught me not the way they teach like this.
Where you slide, you put your, pack your foot down and slide it over for the second beat.
That's the, the banjo player. How do you do? That's the Bill Russell piano.
That's the noise. That's the noise. Now, golf call it. He plays piano, yeah. He still play piano then, I guess. What is your first name?
Gabriel, Clarence Gabriel. Clarence Gabriel. You still play banjo, do you think? I still can play. You can play but you don't have a banjo.
Oh. We like to interview you some of these days too when you have time. We do this with Tulane University trying to get the history of the old time music. All of the jazz musicians that we can find.
You want one of those photographs? Is he on one of those? No. We don't have a photograph with him.
Or the band. You don't have a photograph with a band. We got a different picture to Ruth. You could get it.

When we interview you, maybe we can make a copy of that someday. Is there anything else about Jim Humphrey's teaching that you can remember? You mentioned about the counting and the method. About how long did the lessons last?
The lessons last a half an hour. Was he very strict?
Yeah, he was strict. He was strict.

Now, I went to him, that was around, I was 19, 20. And I stayed with him until around 21, or the first part, middle part of 22 or something like that. Well then, I got in this military band and they had a man, Professor Chalamet, I heard of him. See? Well after, so I stopped taking lessons with Professor Humphrey. While being in his band, he was teaching his band. So I started taking private lessons from Chalamet.

Well, you get back because, of course, some of the Humphreys are still living, the grandchildren, and Willie is still living, the son of your professor too. But I wonder, did he ever play any instrument at your lessons? Did you know what he was best on? What he... Trumpet. Trumpet was his main instrument. Did he ever play that during your lessons? No.
He used to go around with this little club band that he had. With the club band, he played C. Clown.
Could he play any of the other instruments?
Could he play all the other instruments? He could play violin too.
Could play that. I know young Willie plays violin too, or did once. He still has a violin.
Did he have anything to say about your mouthpiece at all?
Yes, he did always need to get a certain type of mouthpiece, and I drew it.
What mouthpiece?
Not too... Oh, not at the name of it. I forgot that. But it was a small, not too big mouthpiece.
A large rim or a narrow rim?
It had a deep cup, and the rim wasn't so very wide. And as far as the name of the mouthpiece... I forgot that.
Do you remember the name of your trombone?
I had a... I bought the trombone... I think it was a... A Holden. That's fine.

One of the best ones I had. It was a Holden. You know if Professor Humphrey recommended a big bell or a little bell, did he ever talk anything about that? No. I've read there's quite a difference supposedly in the tongue, whether it's a big bell or a little bell. Just wondered if anybody paid any attention to that here. No. When did you take up the bakes? How did you happen to change?

I'll tell you how I happened to change on the bakes. By being in this military band, they had two other fellas which you see on there with trombones. And me, I made the fourth one I believe. They didn't select one of those men on there. There was a boy in there. His name is Gus Eli Show. He's on that picture. He wanted to form an orchestra, which he did. What we used to rehearse all the time was the three trombones. So they said that that was too many trombones for about a ten piece band. They only had two trumpets. They couldn't use three trombones. So they didn't have no bakes. So they said to me, well why not you get a bakes? Well I didn't know where to get a bakes from. Things was kind of tight at that time. That was, let me see, that must have been around 24 I think. 25, 20, yeah, around 23. 23 I think it was. Well what I did, I know you all heard of Dave Poiton. Oh yes. Well Dave used to rent instruments.
That's right, I remember.

Well I, the maker of a hoistel on a Sunday evening, I went and borrowed a bass from Dave Poiton, 75 cents. Got it on the street call. Made that rehearsal, we were right here on Ivorville. That's where this father was living. Either he was living there or his sister was living there. I think he was living around here. But they had a piano over there.
Is that the first time you ever played it? First time. Right at the rehearsal.
And I didn't know anything about it.
Did you try to bow it or pick it in those days? Tried to bow it.

Well, so then I had to learn something about the bass. So I went on to a fellow, he was, at one time, he was a good violin player, you might have heard of him, Wendell McNeil. Oh yes. Well I'd taken bass lessons onto him. He was playing bass at that time. I stayed with him about a year. Then I went out for myself and practiced, from what little I knew about music, from the trombone. Yeah. And that's how I came along. And with him and his brother, we used to practice, like I said, with that trio. The Gabriel trio. All in that time, you see. And fooling with this other band at the same time. And I was like, I'm a good guy. So then when we got together fully after this band broke up, they never did succeed. And all they did was the hoisting. Never played one job during the whole time. He was the hoisting. I'd say maybe a year or so. Just the hoisting.
Is the trombone the player the leader? No, the trumpet player.
Oh, the trumpet player. He was the trumpet player.
Remember his name?

Oh yeah. Gus Eli Show. Oh yeah. Well, he never did. The only band he ever played in was this. Big military. Military band there. So that's when we got this, went on with this trio. And we did very well. We used to play music. Take orchestration and give him the banjo part. My brother and I would take the clarinet. And we used to play an orchestration with those three pieces from top to bottom. Is that right, Clarence? Yeah. That's really right. Oh, wow. And when Three Little Boys came out, we were playing in a speakeasy back on Computer Street. That was during Prohibition time. When Three Little Boys came out. We didn't buy that. We just picked it up and played it. And then Gus used to say, you say, you sound just like the fella playing on the record with Duke Ellington. I was playing the same thing. I was playing the same part. After we played it a while, then we bought the orchestration.

Well, there's one thing I forgot to ask about Professor Humphrey's lessons. Did he ever let you work on any of the little popular tunes, any of those late numbers that came out? Did he ever give you anything like that? Well, yeah.
He always tried to advance your picture up.
I knew they wouldn't be in the Carl Fisher book. I wondered if you had some popular late songs and all too at that time.
Well, I think that if you could get somebody maybe would give you or lend you a part, you'd bring it there.
He would help you. He'd help you with any kind of music at all. I thought he might have stuck mostly to the marches and the Method book and not let you work on other kinds.

That's why he told me I was wasting my time fooling with a violin. He wanted me to get on an instrument that I could get out of. I played several jobs from Tronc Wonder with my father-in-law and others. I played Daphonis with him. This fellow here where I'm playing the bass horn, where I play the trombone with him. Oh, yeah. Yeah.

T-boy. T-boy. That was T-boy. Yeah. T-boy. Yeah. We might look at that picture if you don't mind for a minute and tell us who else is on there. Last week Joe Harris told us he got a little mixed up on it. He thought it was Riley. He thought it was something. Riley or somebody on trumpet. I forget. But his father I think is on there, isn't it? Yeah. Mr. Harris. Yeah, his dad is on there. Yeah, yeah. Well, that's the only ones that I know their name. Now, there's a man I know you know.

I just passed his picture. Yeah, we can come back to those. Oh, yeah. Oh, Jimmy Noon, yes. Oh, yes. Did you know him? Yeah. You knew him. I wonder if you could tell us anything about him. Well, no, I couldn't. I just knew him by seeing him playing, you know. I see.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. There's the picture there. And your copy says... Jazz concert. And it wouldn't. Oh, yeah. Is that at the auditorium or something? Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.

Yeah. It's the National Jazz Foundation. Mm-hmm. Let me look at that program just for a minute while you have it there. Does it tell anything else? You know, was there any other groups from New Orleans on there?
Well, I guess it was all...
I don't know what he called that. I don't know.
What's he called that? I don't know. What's he called that?
Sidney Desvinge's big band. Yeah, there it is. Yeah. Sidney Desvinge's big band. And Shuffle Rhythm, After Hours, Back Beat Boogie, C.C. Rider. !
He played all that. Oh, yes.

Sidney Desvinge. Sidney Desvinge. Teddy Wilson. Benny Goodwin's quartet. Let's see what else the Sidney Desvinge's band played. C.C. Rider with Myrtle Jones. And Good Morning Blues with Myrtle Jones. And I once made some records that were singing both of those numbers. Years ago, C.C. Rider, it was never issued. And Pistol Packin' Mama. And then Teddy Wilson played solos in the quartet. This other Dixieland band, I guess that was a group. Wait, no, here's Pinky on his New Orleans jazz band. Yeah, that's what I was. Panama with Monk Hazel. High Society with Irving Fazella. Basin Street with Claire Nunn. So they had several bands from New Orleans on there, too. Yeah. Yeah, then Benny Goodman and his quartet was a band. The quartet was there. They broadcast part of it then. WDSU broadcast. Yeah, let's see if there's a tell what year that was. Yeah, it's been a tell.
What do you call them, what is that?
See, maybe on the front cover, let's see if it tells. Yeah, 1944. October 4th and 5th. There were two concerts there. 1944.
The Auditorium. National Jazz Foundation.

Okay, excuse the interruption. I thought as long as we had that, I was interested to see what other groups were there that night. Now let's see, this is Remy Golden Leaf Orchestra. Is that the, that's Joe Harris's father? Yeah. And who is the banjo? That's Eddie Dawson. That's what I thought, that's what the Harold Dejan does. And you're over here on tuba. You don't know the other sax players. I don't know. You know the girl that's playing piano. Yeah, it's Louise Delvar. She's dead. Oh, she's dead. Louise, how is the last name? Do you know how it's spelled? How do you pronounce it? My wife can tell you. I can never pronounce or spell those French names.
My wife can spell that. How's it pronounced again?
How do you say it? Delvar. Delvar. Delvar. Delvar. And you don't know this trombone then I guess? Yeah, that's George of Jamont. Oh yes. That's a French one too.
Harold Dejan doesn't remember. Yeah George of Jamont.
Do remember the drummer?

Yeah, that's McGee. I don't know what his father meant. Joseph Jamon. Oh yes. Harold Dejean. Do you remember the drummer? Yeah, that's McGee. I don't know. He's four years old. That's right. I think Joe Harris said that too. About when was that? Do you remember what year that would be? This was around 31.

1931. That late, was it? And you say you played trombone too with this same group? No, not with that group. With this fella here, this trumpet player. Where did he get that name T-boy? Do you remember?
Well, from his daddy, you see. That's a French name.
Means little. Little boy. That's what I thought.
Honey, tell me a minute. That's my wife, Mr. Russell.
Hello, Mr. Russell. Let me see you. Mr. Collins.
He wants to know how to spell that Delva. Oh, I want to know.
The lady that plays piano.
She has a big beat. Yeah, he's a big beat. Yeah.

She was also an organist. At first, Harold Dejean, I thought that was May someone. I forget her last name. Oh. Some pianist, but the name of May, that lives uptown around Jackson. So I thought maybe we'd get to talk to her. Oh, yeah, yeah. But if she's dead, of course, we'll never get to see her. I thought it'd be interesting to have her name down right and know how to spell it.
Yeah, she was also an organist. She was our organist at St. Catharine Church. At the church. Oh, for me.
Is that the one up on Tulane? Yeah. The big church there. She was the organist. That's right. She was our organist. She must have been a very good musician. She was. Very good.
Oh, yes. That's good.
Louise, I'll put it on here so in case I lose a slip of paper. D-E-L-V-A-I-L-L-E. Louise Del Vail or something. Del Vail. Del Vail. I can't pronounce it French.
It looks like Louise Del Vail. Well, that's the way you would pronounce it probably in English, but it's French. You've got to say Del Vail.
To return to this band again, T-Boy Hermes Band, do you know where they played? Or where that picture was taken? Was that some nightclub?
Right. This picture was taken on the Pelican.
Oh, the Pelican. Pelican dance hall, yes. You remember when the Pelican was. Yes.
That is not my instrument, but I had one. Well, you've got to ask too. That was on a fella named Twenna.
Twenna, I don't know.

Oh, when I taken this, I had a tuba. I started that in 28 with this. Let's see. Which tour was that? With this band. I don't forget his name. He was a, I think he was a foreigner too. He was from British Honduras. I just remember his first name. Now this is the band caused me to have a tuba.
This is the O'Day-Jean Black Diamond Orchestra, 1928 the picture says. Can you tell us who the members of that are? That's Eddie Pearson.
Oh, Standing in Back, in the Dark Coat. That's Leo Dejean.
Oh, on trumpet, yes.
That's Alvin McNeil. He is the nephew of the one that I spoke about. Oh, yes. Alvin, he was a very good musician. And he's next to the drums. He's also dead. And the drummer is...
That's Sidney Monahue, you know him.
Oh, yeah, sure. Yeah. Let me see that. He's small, you see, that's why. I would never know him from there. He's very... Now this is Edward Johnson.
In the sax, yes.
He's active, yes. Now that's Herbert Larry.
Oh, yes, on the piano. And you mentioned you'd worked with him, was it, for 17 years?

Yeah, I started from 32. Worked with him 17 years. 17 years. Now this is a boy named Reece Corbett. He's not here, he lives in California, and I think he's stopped playing music a good number of years.
Tenor sax, I believe he has.
Tenor, that's right. Now that's... His name is Reuben McClellan.
The banjo.
Yeah, he don't play anymore. He drives a truck for the Southern Demolishing Company.
Oh, yeah. Still around town. Mm-hmm, we are.
Now that's me. Oh, yeah. Don't look like it.
With a mustache. Now that's Harold. You look quite different. Well, that's Harold Deshawn right there. Yeah, he looks different too. You saw that picture, didn't you, Ralph?
Now that's a... He has a clear up net.
He was a dancer.
Oh, yes.
I've heard of him too, yeah. He was a dancer. That's a good picture of him. See, Leo played violin also.
He had his violin there. That's Harold Bunch. He was a very good musician too. I don't know if he still plays. He lives in California. I think he does some.
I don't think he's very active, but I think he still plays some. He was very good.
He was very strict for a youngster. He was young. But he controlled that band.
Where did you all work mostly? Do you remember? Well, we worked on the Pelican.

At that time, the Pelican, the Economy Hall, Autocrat. They did quite a bit of work. Yes. Now, they might have... You might have heard of a band. It was very famous called the Sunny South. Oh, yes. Well, this band was formed. The Sunny South was formed from this band. From that, yes. You had Dajon, Pearson, Montague. I think that was all. Now, they had Richard McLean. He played guitar with them. And the bass player, I just remember who they had on the bass. But this was the band that caused me to fall asleep that the string bass was antique. Yeah.
A lot of them began changing. I had to get a...

But we never taken no picture with it. I had to get a bass on it. Well, I didn't get a sousaphone. Just an up-up band. I had a German... No, a German helicon bass. It comes around. Oh, it still wrapped around.
Yeah.
It wraps around and the bell came out.
Oh, okay. Yeah. Similar to the sousaphone, don't you? Yeah.
Well, I happened to find a good one in the... in a pawn shop, you see. That's why. I used that helicon bass. I played with Clayton. Kid Clayton.
Could you just pick that up yourself? And Kid Renee.
No, I went under professor with the bass horn. The bass horn.
Chalinday? Went to... No. Humphrey again?
No, wait. He was... He wasn't exactly a teacher, but he was a very good musician.
What was Joe's name, Clarence?
The bass horn player. Joe Howard. Oh, yes. Joe Howard, sure. Yeah. I'd taken bass horn lessons.
Louis Armstrong says he taught him on the boat, too. So I guess he was sort of a teacher, too. He used to help him with his music.

He was, but only at that time I don't think he was born by teaching too much. Well, he played... He also played with the demand band when he was in there. They taught him a lot, you know. Of course, he started playing banjo with Amos Raleigh. And you'll get all that.

You'll get your whole life down sometimes, do you? You got time, do you? You got time? Yeah. Do you remember any other jobs that you had much? You mentioned Pelican and all those... Did you stay there quite a while? Did you play there every week? No, no, only spots. Just spot jobs.

Only spots nights, you know. When the other bands wouldn't be there that they had. Because at that time I think Walter Pichon was playing up there. And sometimes we played with other bands. Two bands. Yeah. Contests.
And this band then came before the other T-Boy Ramey.
Oh yeah. That's 28.
I thought the other was in... It looked like an older picture.

Yeah, yeah. It looked like I said. If that other band wouldn't have... Some of the fellas drifted like me. I went and played with Clayton because he was in the jazz field with the Dixieland, you see. And he was playing a lot more, getting a lot more work than they were. Because they had a big band. Yes.
See how many are in there? Was Cook a regular member? Did he just sing with you sometimes as an entertainer? Or was he a regular member? He was a regular member.
He was. He was.
Because he contracted a lot of jobs for them. Seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven pieces. That's a pretty big band, counting the Cook. Yeah.
Yeah.
We played at a couple of hotels. Mont Leon. For different sororities, you know, like that. Yes. You say he went to Clayton. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No.
You only just started using the bass horn about 927? That's right, Ron. Ain't that right, Ron? It's around 26 or 27, something like that.

Then everybody wanted to change? Everybody, everybody. All the bands was with bass. They told you your bass, your string bass is old-fashioned. I know men that were... What famous bass violin players went on tubas, like Henry Kimball, Jimmy Johnson. All those fellas were playing tubas at that time.
They all went on tubas.

None of the bands, they didn't. They seen all the other bands, all the bands that used to come here, they had sousaphones, you see? They'd say the band looked out of deep. That's why they didn't want it.
How long did that last?
Well, that lasted, I'll say, up until around... Somewhere around 35 or something like that. Then they started dying away. The string bass would start coming back.
Did you get rid of your bass then? The string bass? Yeah, you kept it. You're wise to do that. I never did.
I'll tell you what I did do when I bought this bass I have here. I bought that bass from O'Hara. I got rid of the bass on that I had. That was in the bass. I traded it for the string bass.
Oh, well I think I went to your...
They wasn't used.
Did you ever play any parades in any brass bands in those days? I played with Rene, yeah.
Kid Rene's brass band.

Kid Rene. Yeah, Kid Rene. This other T-Boy Rene, a similar name, at that time was he in the Eureka band? When I heard him, he was in the Eureka band. T-Boy. T-Boy, that was quite late though. I just wondered...
Yeah, he played in the Eureka band. During the years that you played with him too?

I tried, yeah. Because he was the leader of that too, wasn't he? Yeah. Did you play any other bands? Tell me a little bit more about Kid Rene's brass band too while we think of it. Was it a regular organized band or did he just pick up whenever he could?
No, he never had an organized brass band. He wasn't organized. Well how many pieces did he usually use? He used to use 10. Ten.
What period, Bell, was that when you were playing with his brass band? When would that be?
Well that was around 29.
What do you have, two trombones, three trumpets?

Two trombones, two trombones, three trumpets, he had a baritone, alto, bass, climbing, two drums. They didn't use no saxophones at that time in no brass band. That's why I tell my fellas today, they don't have no brass bands because they used too many saxophones. They don't produce the music like the baritone and that alto did. After me. I don't think so either. Sax tone changes the band completely. You got a couple of them.
And they had some alto and baritone players in those days. Do you remember who some of them were?

One was, I don't remember the alto, I don't remember one alto player, he just died. Paul Barberin's father and Cisador Barberin. He was one and Adolf Alexander, I don't know if you remember. I know his son, no. His daddy, I mean the dad. Well he played a good baritone too, the son. And what he had several other guys, but I mean, yeah, there's one fella, he's, I think he must be there too, Georgia Hooker. He was from Alexandria. He was formerly a trumpet player. He was a good baritone player. Now they had one fella, he played trombone, he used to also play baritone. Buddy Johnson. Oh yes. And, what's this guy's name? Clarence, what's that guy, that trombone player's name used to play with Rene Harrison? Harrison Bradley. Yeah, Harrison Bradley. He was a baritone and trombone player. So he was very good. I don't know if he's dead or on the left. Is he dead? I think he is.
I think so, yeah, I'm sure he does. Harrison Barnes, who died last year, used to play trombone. And I know he played with Hooker, he told us about him. I guess he played baritone horn some too.
Yeah.
There must have been quite a few around that we never got to hear.
Oh yeah, they had a fella, I don't know his name, but Alexander's daddy, that's where he gets the name, they call him Tats. That's from his daddy, he used to call him Taton. Oh yeah.
What does that mean? What does that mean?
Taton, no I don't know what that means.
Nothing special.
I don't know what that means. I know it's just a nickname they call him.

It must have a meaning though, but I didn't know it. Now he played in the Excelsior band. He played baritone and they had a fella who used to play, Al Tober, I don't know his name. You know y'all never get much on the Excelsior band.
No, not very many of those fellas are having.
Charles Moret was the leader.
Yeah, I've heard of him. Yeah.
And this, Harrison, Vaughn, and Buddy Johnson was the trombone player. And T.O. played Clarence. Oh yeah. Young Till. Well Lewis played in that band too. Louis Armstrong.
Oh wow, yeah. And he talks about old man Moret.
That's it, he played in the Excelsior band. Yeah. Peter Bocards too played in the Excelsior band.

segments.title: Birth in New Orleans, 1902
segments.summary: Lanoix gives his birth date and the Garden District neighbourhood where he was born.

segments.title: Father the guitarist and the forgotten violinist
segments.summary: His father played guitar and worked with a famous violinist whose name Lanoix cannot recall; no one else in the family played music.

segments.title: Starting trombone with Jim Humphrey, 1919
segments.summary: He took up music at about 17; a cousin gave him a violin but Humphrey steered him to trombone.

segments.title: Gabriel in-laws and the Gabriel trio
segments.summary: Marrying into the Gabriel musical family drew him into music; he describes the family and the banjo, bass and clarinet trio.

segments.title: Humphrey's lessons and his club orchestra
segments.summary: Details of the lessons: twice a week, 50 cents, at Humphrey's home, and the club orchestra rehearsing at members' houses.

segments.title: Humphrey's method and teaching style
segments.summary: The Carl Fischer method book, singing and counting numbers, foot-tapping, and half-hour strict lessons.

segments.title: Leaving Humphrey for Chalamet; Humphrey's instruments
segments.summary: He studied with Humphrey until about 1922, then took private lessons from Chalamet in the military band; Humphrey's main instrument was trumpet but he played others.

segments.title: Mouthpiece and trombone make
segments.summary: Humphrey's advice on mouthpiece and the make of his trombone, a Holton, and bell size.

segments.title: Borrowing a bass from Dave Poiton for a rehearsal
segments.summary: Too many trombones in Gus Eli Show's ten-piece band, so Lanoix borrowed a bass for 75 cents and played it for the first time at rehearsal.

segments.title: Learning bass and the Gabriel trio in Prohibition
segments.summary: He took bass lessons from Wendell McNeil, the rehearsal band never played a job, and the trio played from orchestrations, including Three Little Boys in a speakeasy.

segments.title: Popular tunes in Humphrey's lessons
segments.summary: Humphrey would help students with popular music if they brought parts, and urged an instrument with more work.

segments.title: Looking at a photograph and Jimmy Noone
segments.summary: Interviewers study a photo with Joe Harris's father; Lanoix knew Jimmy Noone only from seeing him play.

segments.title: The 1944 National Jazz Foundation concert program
segments.summary: They read a concert program listing Sidney Desvignes, Teddy Wilson, Pinky's band and others, dated October 1944.

segments.title: The Golden Leaf Orchestra photo and Louise Delvaille
segments.summary: Identifying band members of a 1931 photo and spelling the name of pianist and church organist Louise Delvaille.

segments.title: T-Boy Hermes band at the Pelican; taking up tuba
segments.summary: The photo was taken at the Pelican; Lanoix describes a band that led him to take up tuba around 1928.

segments.title: The 1928 Black Diamond Orchestra photo, member by member
segments.summary: Lanoix names the members of the Dejan Black Diamond Orchestra photo, including Herbert Larry, with whom he worked 17 years from 1932.

segments.chapter: Bass horn, tubas and Kid Rena
segments.title: Where the band worked, the Sunny South, and the helicon bass
segments.summary: The band played the Pelican, Economy Hall and Autocrat; the Sunny South grew from it; he bought a German helicon bass from a pawn shop.

segments.chapter: Bass horn, tubas and Kid Rena
segments.title: Playing with Kid Clayton and Kid Rena; bass horn lessons from Joe Howard
segments.summary: He played with Clayton and Rena, took bass horn lessons from Joe Howard, and the interviewers mention Louis Armstrong's training.

segments.chapter: Bass horn, tubas and Kid Rena
segments.title: Spot jobs at the Pelican and why he left for Clayton
segments.summary: Pelican work was only spot jobs; he left for Clayton's busier Dixieland band; the big band played hotels and sororities.

segments.chapter: Bass horn, tubas and Kid Rena
segments.title: Switch from string bass to tuba, c. 1927
segments.summary: Bands wanted sousaphones and string bass was considered old-fashioned until about 1935, when it returned.

segments.chapter: Bass horn, tubas and Kid Rena
segments.title: Kid Rena's brass band, 1929
segments.summary: He played in Rena's unorganized ten-piece brass band and objects to saxophones in brass bands.

segments.chapter: Bass horn, tubas and Kid Rena
segments.title: Alto and baritone players, Excelsior band and Manuel Gabriel
segments.summary: Lanoix recalls baritone and alto players, the Excelsior band led by Charles Moret, and Manuel Gabriel on clarinet.

segments.title: Identifying the old brass band photograph
segments.summary: Lanoix names the members of a torn brass band photo, including Martin Gabriel and others.

segments.title: Peter Claver council, uniforms and Chaligny's band
segments.summary: The photo was taken near the parish prison; the band belonged to Knights of Peter Claver at St. Catherine's; Humphrey doubted the band was ready for the street.

segments.title: Chaligny's students and nephew Clarence Ford
segments.summary: Who practiced with the band, then a nephew who plays with Fats Domino.

segments.title: Identifying the lodge band photograph
segments.summary: Lanoix names members of a large picture of mixed Corpus Christi and St. Catherine bands.

segments.title: Counting the musicians: two bands in one photograph
segments.summary: Interviewers count the musicians and conclude the picture shows two bands plus the uniform rank.

segments.title: Lodge parades and Lanoix's 1922 initiation
segments.summary: The band played at initiations; the picture may date from the day he was initiated in June 1922.

segments.title: Five months in Detroit, McCluskey's Tavern
segments.summary: A photo of his in-laws' sons playing at a Detroit tavern where he worked about four months.

segments.title: Herbert Larry's big band and the trio
segments.summary: Larry's band reached 14 men with two basses; they sort out which photo shows the trio.

segments.title: Naming the members of Larry's 1940 band
segments.summary: Lanoix identifies members of Larry's 14-piece band, including Carroll Levine, and counts them.

segments.title: Longest jobs and where the band travelled
segments.summary: No long engagements; spot jobs around Louisiana, Baton Rouge and sorority dances.

segments.title: Why he moved from trombone to bass; Piron's trio
segments.summary: He repeats that the three-trombone band had no bass, and mentions playing string bass with Piron's trio at a country club and the Royal Palm Garden.

segments.title: Records with Charlie Love, concert pictures and closing
segments.summary: Brief talk of records made with Charlie Love, concert pictures, and the tape winding down.
